questions.prompt: A coil acts like a magnet when its circuit is switched on. What creates its magnetic field, and why does switching the current off change it?
questions.answer: Moving electric charges in the current produce the magnetic field. Switching off the current removes that source of the coil's field.
questions.hint: What is flowing through a powered wire? Connect that flow to the magnetic field.

questions.prompt: A friend says a refrigerator magnet needs a hidden battery. Explain why a permanent magnet can have a magnetic field without an external electric circuit.
questions.answer: Electrons have magnetic moments, including an intrinsic spin contribution. Their organized magnetic moments can give a material a lasting field without an external battery.
questions.hint: Think about electrons inside the material. They have magnetic properties even without a battery-powered circuit.

questions.prompt: You cut a bar magnet in half. Will one piece have only a north pole? Predict what each piece will be like and explain.
questions.answer: Each piece has a north and south pole. Cutting the material does not isolate a single pole; its magnetic organization still produces both poles.
questions.hint: Do smaller magnets still have two ends with different magnetic behavior?

questions.prompt: Two iron samples look identical, but only one is magnetized. How can magnetic domain alignment explain the difference?
questions.answer: In the magnetized sample many domains align, so their effects add. In an unmagnetized sample domain orientations largely cancel overall.
questions.hint: Compare domains pointing together with domains pointing in different directions.

questions.prompt: A magnetic crane is too weak. Keeping current and coil length the same, would adding more wire turns strengthen it? Explain the physical reason.
questions.answer: Yes. With the same current and coil length, more turns contribute magnetic fields that add together and strengthen the coil's field.
questions.hint: Each turn contributes a magnetic field. What happens when those contributions reinforce one another?

questions.prompt: You reverse the battery connections to an electromagnet. What happens to its north and south poles, and why?
questions.answer: The poles swap because the current reverses, reversing the magnetic field direction.
questions.hint: Follow this chain: battery connection → current direction → field direction.

questions.prompt: A magnet sits motionless beside a fixed coil connected in a closed circuit. Your partner expects a continuous current. Explain what must change to induce current.
questions.answer: The magnetic flux through the coil must change. Moving the magnet relative to the coil is one way. A steady magnet and fixed loop alone do not give continuous induced current.
questions.hint: Compare holding the magnet still with moving it toward the loop. What changes through the loop?

questions.prompt: A magnet moves toward a coil, but the wire circuit has a gap. Can there be an induced voltage? Can a sustained current flow? Explain the difference.
questions.answer: Changing flux can induce voltage, but the gap prevents a sustained current around the circuit. Current needs a closed conducting path.
questions.hint: Separate voltage from current. Which one requires a closed conducting path?

questions.prompt: The ship's fan is an electric motor. Explain its energy conversion and how magnets and current can make its rotor turn.
questions.answer: A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical motion. A magnetic field exerts forces on the current-carrying coil, arranged to produce a turning effect.
questions.hint: Name the energy input and output, then connect current in a field to a force.

questions.prompt: In the same motor geometry, you reverse only the current while keeping the permanent magnetic field the same. Predict the change in turning effect and explain.
questions.answer: Reversing the current reverses the magnetic force on the coil and thus its turning effect in the same geometry.
questions.hint: The force direction depends on current direction as well as field direction.

questions.prompt: A hand-cranked generator lights a lamp. Where does the electrical energy come from, and what makes a voltage appear in its coil?
questions.answer: Mechanical work from your hand supplies the energy. Rotation changes magnetic flux through a coil, inducing voltage; a closed circuit lets current light the lamp.
questions.hint: The generator does not create energy. What supplies it, and what changes as the coil rotates?

questions.prompt: A motor and a generator can contain similar magnetic parts. Explain how their intended energy conversions differ.
questions.answer: A motor takes electrical energy in and produces mechanical motion. A generator takes mechanical motion in and produces electrical energy.
questions.hint: Trace the energy input and output separately for each machine.

questions.prompt: Compare electron motion in a battery-powered DC circuit with electron motion in an AC circuit. What does alternating actually mean?
questions.answer: In DC the average electron drift is in one direction. In AC the drift reverses direction repeatedly; electrons move back and forth rather than continuously around one way.
questions.hint: Contrast one-direction drift with repeated reversal, not fast versus slow electrons.

questions.prompt: A student says every generator must supply AC because wall outlets supply AC. Explain the useful classroom comparison and correct the overgeneralization.
questions.answer: Batteries supply DC; the electrical grid supplies AC. A generator's design determines its output, so generators can supply AC or DC depending on construction and rectification.
questions.hint: Separate the familiar grid example from a claim about every possible generator design.
